question: You need to store a collection of user IDs where you frequently check whether the collection already contains a given ID, across a large number of IDs, and order does not matter. Which data structure is most appropriate?
options: Set<Int>, because it offers average O(1) membership checks compared to O(n) for an Array.
Array<Int>, because arrays are always faster than sets for any operation.
Dictionary<Int, Int>, since dictionaries are required for uniqueness.
A tuple of Ints, since tuples have fixed size.
explanation: Set is backed by a hash table, giving average O(1) membership tests, which is far more efficient than an Array's O(n) linear search for large collections where order doesn't matter.

question: You are modeling a Point type used throughout a graphics app, copied frequently and never needing identity comparison or inheritance. Should it be a struct or a class, and why?
options: A class, because classes are always more memory-efficient for small types.
A struct, because value semantics avoid unexpected shared mutation when copies are passed around, and no identity or inheritance is needed.
A class, because only classes can conform to protocols.
A struct is not possible, since Point has more than one property.
explanation: Struct value semantics mean each copy is independent, preventing accidental shared mutation between unrelated parts of the graphics code; Point also has no need for reference identity or inheritance.

question: In a SwiftUI app following MVVM, where should the logic for validating a signup form (e.g., checking password length and email format) live?
options: Directly inside the View's `body` property, since SwiftUI views are supposed to contain all logic.
In the Model, since Models must contain all app logic regardless of type.
In the ViewModel, which exposes validation results as published properties for the View to read, keeping the View focused on layout.
It does not matter; MVVM has no guidance on where validation logic belongs.
explanation: MVVM keeps Views declarative and focused on layout; business and validation logic belongs in the ViewModel, which exposes results (e.g., via @Published properties) for the View to display.

question: You have Circle, Square, and Triangle structs that each need to compute an area, but they otherwise share no data. What is the most idiomatic Swift design to require this shared capability?
options: Create a base class `Shape` and have each type inherit from it, since only classes can share behavior.
Put all three shapes' properties into one giant struct with optional fields.
Use a single enum with cases for each shape and no shared protocol.
Define a `Shape` protocol with an `area` requirement, and have each struct conform to it.
explanation: Since the types are unrelated structs with no shared implementation, a protocol requirement is the idiomatic Swift way to express a shared capability without forcing inheritance or a class hierarchy.

question: You are designing error handling for a function that parses user input and can fail for several distinct, specific reasons (empty input, invalid format, out-of-range value). What is the most idiomatic way to model these errors in Swift?
options: Define an enum conforming to `Error` with a case for each distinct failure reason, optionally with associated values for extra context.
Use a single `Bool` return value to indicate success or failure.
Throw the same generic `NSError` for every failure case.
Return an optional value and rely on `nil` to represent all failure reasons uniformly.
explanation: An Error-conforming enum with one case per failure reason lets callers pattern-match on the specific cause in a catch block, and associated values can carry extra diagnostic context.

question: You need to frequently look up a User object by its unique username string, and you have tens of thousands of users. Which data structure is best suited?
options: Array<User>, searched linearly by username each time.
Dictionary<String, User>, keyed by username, for near O(1) lookups.
Set<User>, since sets support key-based lookup.
A sorted array with manual binary search reimplemented from scratch, since Dictionary cannot use String keys.
explanation: Dictionary provides near O(1) average-case lookups by key, which is ideal for looking up users by a unique username across a large collection, far outperforming a linear array scan.

question: Multiple SwiftUI views across your app need to observe and react to the same shared shopping cart, where updates from one screen must be visible on all others. Should the cart be modeled as a struct or a class, and why?
options: A struct, because SwiftUI only works with structs for state of any kind.
Either works identically, since SwiftUI copies structs and classes the same way.
A class conforming to ObservableObject, because reference semantics let multiple views share and observe one single source of truth.
A struct wrapped in an array, since arrays provide reference semantics in Swift.
explanation: A shared, mutable model that many independent views must observe and update needs reference semantics; an ObservableObject class lets all views hold a reference to the same single source of truth.

question: You want a single Cache protocol that can store either String or Int values depending on the conforming type, with type safety enforced at compile time. What Swift feature should the protocol use?
options: Store everything as `Any` and cast at the call site.
Use a class instead of a protocol, since protocols cannot vary by type.
Duplicate the protocol once for String and once for Int.
An associated type (e.g., `associatedtype Value`) used in the protocol's requirements.
explanation: An associated type lets a protocol's requirements refer to a placeholder type that each conforming type specifies concretely, giving compile-time type safety without duplicating the protocol or relying on `Any`.

question: You are storing a playlist of songs where order matters and the same song may legitimately appear twice. Which data structure fits, and why not a Set?
options: Array, because it preserves insertion order and allows duplicate elements, while Set enforces uniqueness and has no defined order.
Set, because sets are more memory-efficient regardless of ordering needs.
Dictionary, keyed by song title, since titles are always unique.
Either works identically for this use case.
explanation: Array preserves the order elements were inserted and permits duplicates, both of which a playlist requires; Set would silently collapse duplicate song entries and offers no ordering guarantee.

question: Where should networking code (e.g., URLSession calls to fetch data from an API) typically live in a well-structured SwiftUI MVVM app?
options: Directly inside the SwiftUI View's `body`, triggered every time it re-renders.
In a dedicated service/repository type that the ViewModel calls, keeping networking details out of both the View and the Model.
Inside the Model's stored properties, since Models represent data.
It should be split evenly between the View and ViewModel for redundancy.
explanation: Isolating networking in a dedicated service or repository type keeps concerns separated: the View stays declarative, the ViewModel orchestrates state, and the service encapsulates I/O details, which also improves testability.

question: A team is debugging a bug where updating one Order object in a list unexpectedly appeared to update a different Order displayed elsewhere, because Order was implemented as a class. What is the most direct design fix?
options: Add more `print` statements to the class to track mutations.
Mark all of Order's properties as `static`.
Change Order to a struct, so each copy is independent and mutations to one copy do not affect others.
Wrap every Order instance in an array before use.
explanation: The bug is a classic symptom of unintended reference sharing; switching Order to a struct gives it value semantics, so each copy is independent and mutating one no longer affects others.

question: A view's loading state can be exactly one of: idle, loading, loaded (with data), or failed (with an error). What is the most robust way to model this compared to using several Bool flags like isLoading and hasError?
options: Four separate Bool properties, one for each state, checked independently.
A single Int property where 0, 1, 2, 3 represent each state.
A String property holding the state's name, compared with `==`.
A single enum with cases `idle`, `loading`, `loaded(Data)`, and `failed(Error)`, which makes invalid combinations (like loading and failed at once) unrepresentable.
explanation: Modeling mutually exclusive states as one enum makes impossible combinations (such as isLoading and hasError both true) unrepresentable, unlike independent Bool flags which can drift into inconsistent states.

question: Why can't you use class inheritance to share default behavior across Circle and Square if both are implemented as structs?
options: Structs cannot inherit from other types in Swift; shared behavior across structs must instead be achieved with protocols and protocol extensions.
You can use inheritance with structs, but only up to one level deep.
Structs can inherit, but only from classes, not from other structs.
Inheritance works fine with structs; the limitation only applies to enums.
explanation: Swift structs do not support inheritance at all; to share default behavior across multiple struct types, you use protocols with protocol extensions providing default implementations instead.

question: A function `loadFile(named:)` can fail for several distinct reasons a caller may want to distinguish and handle differently (file not found vs. permission denied vs. corrupted data). Should it return an optional or use `throws`, and why?
options: It should return an optional, since optionals are simpler for callers to handle in all cases.
It should use `throws` with a custom Error enum, since optionals can only represent a single generic "failure," losing the specific reason.
It doesn't matter; optionals and throwing functions convey identical information.
It should return a Bool and rely on a separate global variable to store the error reason.
explanation: An optional collapses every failure into a single nil case, discarding the reason; a throws function paired with an Error enum preserves distinct, pattern-matchable failure cases for callers.

question: What is a key benefit of moving business logic out of SwiftUI Views and into ViewModels, in terms of testing?
options: SwiftUI Views cannot be compiled without a ViewModel, making testing mandatory.
Moving logic to the ViewModel eliminates the need for any testing at all.
ViewModels can be unit tested directly without instantiating any SwiftUI view hierarchy, since they don't depend on the rendering system.
Business logic runs faster when placed in a ViewModel due to compiler optimizations.
explanation: Because ViewModels are plain objects independent of SwiftUI's rendering system, they can be instantiated and unit tested directly, without needing to render a view hierarchy.

question: A codebase has `NetworkManager.shared` used directly throughout the app, and unit tests that exercise networking code are flaky and slow because they hit the real network. What design change best improves testability?
options: Add a global boolean flag `isTesting` that `NetworkManager.shared` checks internally to decide whether to hit the real network
Mark all of `NetworkManager`'s methods as `static` so they can be called without an instance
Increase the test timeout so flaky network calls have more time to succeed
Define a protocol abstracting the networking behavior, inject a conforming implementation (or a mock/test double) into the types that need it, instead of referencing the concrete singleton directly
explanation: Depending on a concrete singleton hardcodes a single, real implementation everywhere it's used, making it impossible to substitute a fast, deterministic test double. Defining a protocol and injecting an implementation (dependency injection) lets tests supply a mock that satisfies the same interface without touching the network.

question: When designing `Codable` models for a JSON API that uses `snake_case` keys (e.g. `"user_name"`) while your Swift properties use `camelCase` (e.g. `userName`), what is the most maintainable approach?
options: Define explicit `CodingKeys` mapping each camelCase property to its snake_case JSON key (or, if the mapping is uniform, set the decoder's `keyDecodingStrategy` to `.convertFromSnakeCase`)
Rename all Swift properties to match the JSON's snake_case naming exactly, violating Swift naming conventions
Manually rewrite every JSON payload in the app to camelCase before decoding
Avoid `Codable` entirely and parse the JSON with manual dictionary subscripting
explanation: `CodingKeys` (or the decoder's built-in snake_case conversion strategy when the mapping is consistent) lets the model keep idiomatic Swift naming while still correctly mapping to the API's actual JSON key names, which is far more maintainable than renaming properties or hand-parsing dictionaries.

question: A screen's state is currently modeled with three independent properties: `isLoading: Bool`, `hasError: Bool`, and `data: [Item]?`. This allows invalid combinations, like `isLoading == true` and `hasError == true` at the same time. What is the recommended redesign?
options: Combine `hasError` and `data` into a single `Any?` property
Replace the independent booleans with a single enum, such as `enum LoadState { case idle, loading, loaded([Item]), failed(Error) }`, so only one state can be represented at a time
Add a fourth boolean, `isValid`, that gets manually kept in sync with the other three
Keep the three booleans but add runtime assertions that fire if an invalid combination occurs
explanation: Multiple independent booleans can represent combinations that don't correspond to any real, meaningful state (like loading and error simultaneously). A single enum with mutually exclusive cases makes illegal states unrepresentable at the type level, since only one case can be active at a time.

question: A single `HomeViewModel` class has grown to handle authentication, feed pagination, notification badges, and settings persistence, all in one file. What is the recommended refactor?
options: Move all of its methods into extensions in separate files, while keeping it as a single type
Convert it to a singleton so any screen can access it without passing references

Split the responsibilities into separate, focused view models (or services) — one per concern — and compose them where the screen actually needs more than one, rather than keeping a single object owning everything
Rename the class to `AppViewModel` to better reflect its broad scope
explanation: A view model that has accumulated unrelated responsibilities (a 'god object') becomes hard to test, reason about, and reuse. Splitting it into smaller, focused types along its actual responsibilities (auth, pagination, notifications, settings) improves testability and keeps each piece's scope clear; renaming or reorganizing into extensions without separating responsibilities doesn't address the underlying coupling.

options: Option A is always preferable because it catches constraint violations earlier at the type's declaration
There is no practical difference between the two approaches
Option B will not compile because extensions cannot add constraints beyond the original type's declaration

Option B is more flexible: it lets `Pair` be used with any type `T`, while only adding the `Comparable`-dependent functionality (like `isOrdered()`) when `T` actually conforms, rather than restricting the whole type upfront
explanation: Constraining the entire type (Option A) forces every use of `Pair`, even ones that never need ordering, to require `Comparable`. Constraining only the extension that needs it (Option B) keeps the base type maximally general while still providing the constrained functionality when it's actually applicable.

question: A multi-stage data pipeline (fetch from network, decode JSON, validate business rules) currently throws a single generic `Error` type from every stage, making it hard for callers to react differently to a network failure versus a validation failure. What design improves this?
options: Define distinct, typed error enums per stage (e.g. `NetworkError`, `DecodingError`-specific cases, `ValidationError`) and propagate them (e.g. via `Result<Value, SpecificError>` or typed `throws`), so callers can pattern-match on the specific failure category
Wrap every error in `NSError` with a numeric code that callers must remember by convention
Have every stage silently return a default value on failure instead of throwing
Combine all possible errors from every stage into one giant catch-all enum with 50+ cases used everywhere in the app
explanation: Using a single opaque error type collapses meaningfully different failure categories into one, forcing callers to guess or inspect strings to react appropriately. Modeling distinct, typed errors per pipeline stage lets callers pattern-match precisely (e.g. retry on a network error, but show a validation message on a validation error) without stringly-typed workarounds.

question: A struct's stored properties are all declared with default internal access, letting any code in the module freely mutate them and potentially violate the type's invariants (e.g. setting a `count` property negative). What design change enforces the invariant while keeping the type easy to use?
options: Convert the struct into a class so ARC can manage its invariants
Make the properties `private(set)` (readable externally, writable only inside the type) and expose controlled mutating methods that validate input before changing state
Make every property `private` and provide no way to read them from outside the type
Leave the properties as they are, but document in a comment that callers should not set invalid values
explanation: Access control is a form of encapsulation: `private(set)` lets external code read the current state (keeping the type easy to consume) while forcing all mutation to go through the type's own methods, which can validate input and preserve invariants instead of relying on caller discipline.

question: Two sibling SwiftUI views need to coordinate through shared state, but a design keeps having `ViewA` hold a direct reference to `ViewB`'s internal view model and calling its methods to keep them synchronized. What is a better architectural pattern?
options: Have `ViewB` poll `ViewA`'s state on a timer instead of being called directly
Use `NotificationCenter` broadcasts for all state coordination between every pair of views in the app
Introduce a shared observable model owned by a common ancestor (or injected via the environment) that both views read from and write to, rather than one view directly referencing another's internals
Merge `ViewA` and `ViewB` into a single monolithic view so there's no coordination problem
explanation: Direct references between sibling views' internals create tight coupling that's hard to test and reason about in isolation. A shared model owned by a common ancestor (or provided through the environment) lets both views depend on a common source of truth without depending directly on each other.

question: When deciding between a `struct` and a `class` for a new type, which heuristic is most accurate?
options: Always prefer `class`, since Swift's ARC makes reference types strictly more efficient than value types in every situation
Always prefer `struct`, since classes are deprecated in modern Swift
The choice never matters because Swift automatically converts between the two as needed for optimization

Prefer `struct` for simple values without a persistent identity that should be copied on assignment; prefer `class` when you need shared mutable reference identity, inheritance, or interoperability with reference-type APIs
explanation: Value types like `struct` fit data that represents an independent value with no shared identity — copies behave independently, which limits accidental shared mutation. Reference types like `class` fit cases needing shared, mutable identity across multiple owners, inheritance hierarchies, or interoperability with reference-based frameworks.

question: A team wants to share common formatting behavior (e.g. `displayName`) across several unrelated model types (`User`, `Organization`, `Product`) that don't share a natural class hierarchy. What is a more flexible design than introducing a shared base class?
options: Define a protocol with the shared requirement and provide a default implementation via a protocol extension, letting each unrelated type (including structs) opt in by conformance rather than inheritance
Force all three types to inherit from a common `NSObject` subclass just to share this one piece of behavior
Duplicate the formatting logic separately in each of the three types
Put the formatting logic in a global free function that takes an `Any` parameter and uses runtime type checks
explanation: A shared base class requires every participating type to fit into a single inheritance hierarchy and rules out value types entirely. A protocol with a default extension implementation lets unrelated types, including structs, adopt the shared behavior purely by conforming to the protocol, without forcing an artificial hierarchy.

question: Code throughout an app calls `Date()` directly wherever the current time is needed, and this makes date-dependent logic (like 'is this offer expired') difficult to test deterministically. What design change improves testability?
options: Skip testing any code path that depends on the current time
Introduce a small protocol (e.g. `DateProviding` with a `now: Date` property), inject an implementation of it wherever the current time is needed, and supply a fixed/fake implementation in tests
Replace all calls to `Date()` with a global mutable variable that tests can set directly from anywhere
Add a `#if DEBUG` branch throughout the codebase that hardcodes a fixed date only in debug builds
explanation: Calling a global, non-deterministic system API like `Date()` directly embeds an untestable dependency throughout the codebase. Abstracting 'the current time' behind an injectable protocol lets production code use the real clock while tests inject a fixed, deterministic value, making time-dependent logic reliably testable.

question: A public API function is declared as `func loadUser() -> User!` (returning an implicitly unwrapped optional) to avoid making callers deal with `Optional`. What is the design problem with this choice?
options: It's a problem only because `User` should be a struct rather than a class
Implicitly unwrapped optionals make the function run faster than a regular optional would

It hides the real possibility of failure from the type system; if loading can fail, callers should receive an `Optional<User>` (or a `throws`/`Result`-based API) so the compiler forces them to handle the failure case explicitly
There is no problem; implicitly unwrapped optionals are the recommended way to simplify any public API's return type
explanation: An implicitly unwrapped optional lets callers use the value without unwrapping syntax, but it also removes the compiler's ability to force them to handle a `nil` case explicitly — deferring a potential crash to whenever the value happens to be `nil`. If failure is truly possible, a genuine `Optional`, `throws`, or `Result`-based signature communicates that honestly and requires callers to handle it.

question: A screen's behavior is currently controlled by three separate booleans: `isEditingEnabled`, `isSavingInProgress`, and `isReadOnlyMode`, and combinations like `isEditingEnabled == true` with `isReadOnlyMode == true` don't make sense but are still possible in code. What is the design smell here, and the fix?
options: There is no design smell as long as unit tests check every boolean combination
The fix is to add a fourth boolean that overrides the other three when they conflict
The booleans should be converted into a single bitmask integer for efficiency

The booleans can represent mutually contradictory states simultaneously; replacing them with a single enum whose cases are mutually exclusive (e.g. `.editing`, `.saving`, `.readOnly`) makes invalid combinations unrepresentable
explanation: Independent booleans can be combined in ways that don't correspond to any valid real-world state, requiring careful, error-prone runtime checks to avoid nonsensical combinations. An enum with mutually exclusive cases guarantees, at compile time, that the screen is always in exactly one valid state.

question: A small app currently has one massive `AppState: ObservableObject` that every single screen observes, even though most screens only care about a small slice of it. What are the tradeoffs of this design compared to smaller, screen-scoped state objects?
options: The single giant object causes every screen to re-render whenever any part of the state changes (since `objectWillChange` fires for the whole object), and it couples unrelated screens together; scoped, per-screen state objects (sharing only genuinely global state) reduce unnecessary re-renders and coupling
There are no meaningful tradeoffs; a single shared `AppState` is always strictly better for performance
Smaller, scoped state objects are impossible to implement in SwiftUI
The giant object is preferable because it guarantees every screen always has perfectly consistent data
explanation: Because any `@Published` change on an `ObservableObject` triggers updates for every observer of that object, a single all-encompassing state object causes unrelated screens to re-render on changes they don't actually care about, and it tightly couples every screen to a single shared type. Scoping state to what each screen actually needs (while still sharing truly global state where appropriate) reduces both problems.

question: A team is designing the boundary between their networking layer and their UI layer. Which approach best isolates the UI from changes in the underlying network/decoding implementation?
options: Make every UI view inherit from a shared `NetworkingViewController` base class that performs requests directly

Have the networking layer expose a small protocol describing the operations the UI needs (e.g. `fetchUser(id:) async throws -> User`), with the concrete implementation (and its `URLSession`/decoding details) hidden behind it, so the UI depends only on the protocol
Have UI code call `URLSession.shared` and decode JSON directly wherever data is needed, for simplicity
Expose the raw `Data` returned by the network call directly to the UI layer and let each screen decode it as needed
explanation: Defining a narrow protocol that describes only the operations the UI actually needs, with the concrete networking/decoding details hidden behind an implementation of that protocol, decouples the UI from how data is fetched or decoded — changes to the underlying implementation (or swapping in a test double) don't require changes to UI code.
